subject: zoology
question_text: Describe the blood circulatory system of Periplaneta in detail and draw a neat and labelled diagram of it.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.21-22, LAQ 7). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. APPEARANCES: the book prints [AP May-17,19], [TS M-16,20], [AP M-15] and [IPE-14]; the 2014 entry has no board because it predates bifurcation. TWO COUNTS DIFFER BETWEEN SOURCES and this card follows the source book: (1) ostia — the book says every chamber EXCEPT the last bears a pair, which gives 12 pairs; other texts print 13 pairs, one for every chamber; (2) alary muscles — the book says one pair per segment and does not give a total, while several texts print 12 pairs. A teacher must settle both before this card is taught. FIGURE SCOPE: the book prints a dorsal view of the 13-chambered heart with alary muscles beside a transverse section showing the sinuses; this card draws the same two views simplified to what a student can reproduce.

steps.label: Open circulatory system
lines: The blood of the cockroach is not held in
closed vessels. It flows freely in the body
spaces called the haemocoel, so the system is
of the open type.
It has three parts — the haemocoel, the heart
and the blood.
It carries digested food, nitrogenous waste
and hormones from one part of the body to
another.
steps.why: Open type is the one word the examiner looks for first, and it explains the rest of the answer: with no closed vessels, the body cavity itself has to be divided into sinuses for the blood to travel through.
common_mistakes: Calling it a closed circulatory system. The blood leaves the heart into open body spaces.
Leaving out the three parts, which set the order of the whole answer.
steps.memory_tip: Open type: the blood flows in the body cavity itself, not in vessels. Three parts to describe — haemocoel, heart, blood.
steps.margin_note: Open type, the haemocoel, and the three parts. Three short lines before the detail starts.

steps.label: Diagram — heart and sinuses

elements.caption: Step 1 — body outline, aorta and the dorsal heart
Step 2 — the 13 chambers and the pairs of ostia
Step 3 — alary muscles on both sides
Step 4 — cross section: body wall and the two diaphragms
Step 5 — heart, gut and nerve cord in the section

steps.why: Two views are needed because the facts live in different directions: the chambers and alary muscles show along the length of the body, and the three sinuses only show in a cross section.
common_mistakes: Drawing the heart on the ventral side. The heart is dorsal, just under the tergal plates.
Drawing fewer than 13 chambers. The number is marked.
Putting the nerve cord in the perivisceral sinus. It lies in the perineural sinus, below the ventral diaphragm.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the long view first with 13 boxes and the alary muscles on the sides, then a small oval cross section beside it with two lines across for the two diaphragms.
steps.margin_note: Label the heart chambers, alary muscles, aorta, both diaphragms and all three sinuses — the labels carry the two marks.

steps.label: Haemocoel and sinuses
lines: Haemocoel: the body cavity filled with blood.
Two horizontal muscular membranes, the dorsal
diaphragm and the ventral diaphragm, divide
it into three sinuses. Both diaphragms carry
valvular pores.
The pericardial sinus lies above the dorsal
diaphragm and surrounds the heart.
The perivisceral sinus lies between the two
diaphragms and surrounds the gut. It is the
largest of the three.
The perineural sinus lies below the ventral
diaphragm and surrounds the nerve cord.
A pair of triangular alary muscles lies in
each segment, on the sides of the body.
steps.why: The three sinuses are named after what each one holds — heart, viscera, nerve cord — so the names themselves give the positions, and the two diaphragms are the boundaries between them.
common_mistakes: Naming the sinuses without saying what each surrounds. The organ inside is what makes the name correct.
Writing that the diaphragms are solid. Both have valvular pores that let blood through.
Forgetting the alary muscles, which pull the dorsal diaphragm and drive the whole circulation.
steps.memory_tip: Named by their contents from top to bottom: peri-CARDIAL heart, peri-VISCERAL gut, peri-NEURAL nerve cord.
steps.margin_note: Two diaphragms, three sinuses with what each surrounds, and the alary muscles. This is the biggest part: two marks.

steps.label: Heart
lines: Heart: a long muscular contractile tube. It
lies dorsally, below the tergal plates,
inside the pericardial sinus.
It has 13 chambers. Each chamber opens into
the chamber in front of it through a valve.
Its hind end is closed. In front it opens
into the aorta.
Each chamber except the last bears a pair of
small openings called ostia, one on each
side of its hind end.
The ostia have valves that let blood pass
only from the pericardial sinus into the
heart.
steps.why: The valves are what make an open system still move blood one way: chamber valves send it forward, ostial valves let it in but not out, so the blood can only travel head-ward.
common_mistakes: Writing that blood leaves the heart through the ostia. The ostia are one-way inlets.
Writing that the hind end opens outside. The hind end is closed; the front end opens into the aorta.
steps.memory_tip: Thirteen chambers, all valves one way: in through the ostia, forward through the chambers, out at the aorta.
steps.margin_note: Position, 13 chambers, closed hind end, aorta in front, ostia and their valves. One mark.

steps.label: Blood (haemolymph)
lines: Blood (haemolymph): colourless, made of
plasma and phagocytic haemocytes.
It has no respiratory pigment, so it plays no
major part in carrying oxygen. The tracheal
system carries the air instead.
Functions of the blood:
It absorbs and distributes digested food.
It carries nitrogenous waste to the excretory
organs.
It carries phagocytes to places of infection.
It carries hormones to their target organs.
steps.why: The absence of a respiratory pigment is the point of this part: it is the reason the cockroach needs a tracheal system, and it separates insect blood from human blood in one line.
common_mistakes: Writing that haemolymph is red or carries oxygen. It is colourless and has no respiratory pigment.
Giving only one function. Four functions are expected: food, waste, defence and hormones.
steps.memory_tip: Colourless blood, no pigment: it carries food, waste, phagocytes and hormones, but not oxygen.
steps.margin_note: Colour, two contents, no pigment, then the four functions as short separate lines. One mark.

steps.label: Path of the blood

lines.text: Heart, aorta, sinuses, back by the ostia

lines: The heart muscles contract and push the blood
into the aorta and then into the head sinus.
From the head sinus the blood passes back
through the perivisceral and perineural
sinuses.
The alary muscles contract and pull the
dorsal diaphragm down, so blood enters the
pericardial sinus.
The alary muscles relax, the diaphragm moves
up, and the blood is forced through the ostia
into the heart. The circulation goes on.
steps.why: This step turns the named parts into one loop, and it shows that the alary muscles, not the heart, are what draw the blood back into the pericardial sinus.
common_mistakes: Writing that the heart draws the blood back in. The alary muscles pull the diaphragm down and do that work.
Ending the answer at the sinuses without closing the loop back into the heart.
steps.memory_tip: Forward by the heart, backward through the sinuses, upward by the alary muscles, inward through the ostia.
steps.margin_note: Four sentences in one direction, ending back at the heart. Write it as a loop, not as a list.

insider_note: The two diagram marks are given for the labels, and the pair most often lost is the two diaphragms with the three sinuses they separate — students draw the 13-chambered heart neatly and then leave the cross section out altogether.
